text: There is a formula that turns the depth of a lake into money.
Who writes something like that, and what happens when the lake falls?
It is item 1500.0000 of the Panama Canal's official tariff.
Feed it the depth of Gatun Lake in feet, and it returns a fresh water surcharge of up to ten percent of everything a ship pays to cross.
The curve bends at one number.
Eighty-two feet.
By the end of this you will have three prices for one cubic metre of the same lake water.
What a household in Panama City paid for it.
What the canal earns on it on an average day.
And what a shipping line paid for it at auction, on the first of September 2026.
They are not close.
And the highest is not what the canal charges anyone.
This is not a queue story; it is a water market, and the canal is the seller.
In February 2026, the median price for an auctioned slot was about fifty-five thousand dollars.
The canal sells most of its daily crossings by booking, but a few go to auction, and anyone can bid.
The canal's administrator puts the typical clearing price before the conflict at a hundred and thirty-five to a hundred and forty thousand.
By March and April it was around three hundred and eighty-five thousand.
Then the chart stops behaving like a chart and starts behaving like a panic.
In August, a gas carrier called the G. Arete took a slot for four point six million dollars.
That record lasted three weeks.
On the first of September 2026, South Korea's SK group paid five point three million dollars to move one ship, the G. Spirit, northbound through the canal.
Not for the cargo.
For the crossing.
Three separate outlets confirm the figure.
At the peak, eighteen bidders chased a single slot, against a normal two or three.
Between a fifth and a quarter of ships were arriving with no booking at all.
A ship that misses a booking either bids, or waits.
Some of them waited eleven days.
Ask the man who runs the canal how the price got there, and the answer is flat.
We do not set prices; the market sets the price.
Eighteen bidders is not a shortage of ships.
It is a shortage of water, priced.
So what does five point three million dollars actually buy?
One transit through the big locks spends an estimated two hundred thousand cubic metres of Gatun Lake.
The Authority publishes its water in millions of cubic metres a day, not gallons per ship.
No primary document of theirs states a per-transit figure, so hold that number as a band, not a measurement.
Where the water comes from is not in doubt.
Gatun Lake is the drinking water for fifty-five percent of Panama's population.
The same lake.
In the drought of 2023, the system was losing ten million cubic metres a day and gaining seven.
Rainfall came in a quarter below the seventy-three-year average.
Lake levels were the lowest since at least 1965.
On the seventh of November that year, the canal cut itself to twenty-four crossings a day, from a normal thirty-four.
The 2024 financial year closed twenty-one percent below the one before it.
And 2026 is not a recovery.
From May to August, rain ran thirty-four percent below average, and inflows forty-four percent below.
The Authority attributes this year to a forecast El Nino, which is weather.
A 2025 study is a different thing entirely.
It simulated the lake with twenty-seven climate models, and found conditions like these become common under high emissions, and do not under low.
That is a projection, not a forecast, and it is not this year's El Nino.
Three prices, same cubic metre.
In 2018, water in Panama City worked out at twenty-one cents a cubic metre.
That is total revenue divided by total volume sold, and it is eight years old.
Second bar, and this is the one nobody else has drawn.
In financial year 2025 the canal ran thirteen thousand four hundred and four transits and took five point seven billion balboas.
Divide that by the water those transits spent, and the canal's own average lands near two dollars thirteen a cubic metre.
Third bar.
Five point three million dollars, divided by the water one transit spends, is about twenty-seven dollars a cubic metre.
Now the caveat that keeps this honest.
Of the canal's thirty-four daily slots, exactly three go to auction.
So twenty-seven dollars prices the last nine percent of capacity, bid up by the ships that arrived unbooked.
It is a scarcity signal, not what the canal charges the fleet.
But even as a signal, it is roughly a hundred times what the household paid.
And here is the part the auction only implies.
The tariff publishes it.
Put August's lake level, eighty-four point three feet, into item 1500.0000, and the surcharge is two percent of tolls.
At eighty-two feet, the bend in the curve, it is five.
At the just-over-seventy-nine feet of the 2023 floor, it is nearly nine.
Plus a flat ten thousand dollars on every ship longer than three hundred feet.
The market took until September 2026 to price this water.
The canal had already written the price down.
One more thing about the record.
The lake did not fall five point three million dollars' worth in a week.
When the canal's administrator names the old price, a hundred and thirty-five thousand dollars, he dates it to before a conflict on the other side of the world.
In a strait that never actually closed.
So the question this episode leaves open is not about rain at all.
How does a strait that stayed open set the price of Panamanian water?
